nameStory: **Note: I'm uncertain about this species identification - Stauridium tetras appears to be a microscopic freshwater algae, not a typical plant that nature explorers would identify in the field.** The name 'Stauridium' comes from the Greek word 'stauros' meaning cross, referring to the cross-shaped arrangement of the algae cells. The species name 'tetras' means 'four,' likely describing the four-celled colonies this tiny organism forms.
description: **Uncertainty flag: This appears to be microscopic algae rather than a macroscopic plant.** Stauridium tetras is a microscopic freshwater green algae that forms tiny four-celled colonies. Each colony is so small you'd need a microscope to see individual cells clearly. In nature, you might notice it as a faint green tinge or film in still freshwater. This is not a plant you'd typically identify during a nature walk, as it requires magnification to observe properly.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Individual colonies are invisible to the naked eye - you'll need at least 100x magnification to see the characteristic four-cell arrangement

idTips.label: Four-cell colonies
idTips.description: Under magnification, cells are arranged in groups of four, often in a cross-like or square pattern

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: Cells contain bright green chloroplasts that give them an emerald appearance under the microscope

idTips.label: Freshwater habitat
idTips.description: Found floating freely in still or slow-moving freshwater - never in saltwater or on land

habitat: **Uncertainty about specific New England distribution.** This microscopic algae is found in still or slow-moving freshwater throughout New England, including ponds, quiet stream backwaters, and temporary pools. It prefers nutrient-rich waters and may be more abundant in areas with some organic matter.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm and nutrients increase from spring runoff. Populations may begin to grow as ice melts.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season in warm waters. May form more noticeable populations in favorable conditions.
seasonality.fall: Populations may persist but growth slows as temperatures drop and daylight decreases.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant or present in very small numbers. May survive as resting stages in sediments.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, billions of these tiny four-celled colonies can live in a single cup of pond water, quietly producing oxygen through photosynthesis just like the giant trees around the pond's edge!
confusionNotes: **Uncertain about similar species.** As a microscopic organism, it could be confused with other small colonial green algae, but the distinctive four-cell arrangement visible under magnification is the key distinguishing feature.
contextualKnowledge: This represents a different type of 'plant' exploration than typical nature walks - it's part of the hidden microscopic world that exists in every drop of pond water. Most nature guides focus on plants visible to the naked eye, making this an unusual subject for field identification.
compareHints: **Uncertain about relatives in the region.** If no other Stauridium species are present in New England, this would be compared with other small colonial green algae in the family Hydrodictyaceae. The four-cell colony arrangement would be the primary distinguishing feature from other microscopic green algae that might form different colony patterns or exist as single cells.
